title: Reporting a School Energy Audit
description: Edit a full informational passage for grammar, punctuation, usage, and clarity.
subject: rla
author: Studo
reviewNotes: Mixed editing passage reviewed for sentence-context fidelity, one-best-answer grammar logic, and GED-style editing transfer.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct capitalization. Here 'environmental science' names the subject generally, not an official course title.

options.text: The Environmental Science class reviewed bills from March.
options.whyWrong: A school subject used generically is usually lowercase unless it is a language or part of a formal course title.

options.text: The environmental science class reviewed bills from march.
The environmental science class reviewed bills from March.
The Environmental science class reviewed bills from March.
options.whyWrong: The generic subject phrase should not be partly capitalized.

explanation.whyCorrect: The generic subject name is lowercase; the month 'March' is capitalized.
explanation.quickTip: Capitalize proper names and calendar names, not ordinary school subjects used generically.

questions.prompt: Choose the clearest pronoun revision: “The class compared the bills with the schedule because it had changed.”

options.text: The class compared the bills with the schedule because it had changed.
options.whyWrong: 'It' could refer to the class, bill set, or schedule.

options.text: The class compared them with it because it changed.
options.whyWrong: The pronouns do not identify the intended nouns clearly.

options.text: It changed, so it compared the bills with the schedule.
options.whyWrong: Both instances of 'it' lack a clear antecedent.

options.text: Because the schedule had changed, the class compared it with the bills.

explanation.whyCorrect: The revision names the changed item, 'schedule,' and keeps the later pronoun reference clear.
explanation.quickTip: When a pronoun could point to multiple nouns, name the intended noun.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct possessive: “The {{blank}} report separates observations from conclusions.”

options.text: student's
options.whyWrong: This shows possession by one student rather than the group.

options.text: students'
students
options.whyWrong: The plural noun does not show possession of the report.

options.text: students's
options.whyWrong: A regular plural ending in s takes only an apostrophe for possession.

explanation.whyCorrect: The report belongs to multiple students, so the plural possessive is students'.
explanation.quickTip: For a regular plural ending in s, add only an apostrophe.

questions.prompt: Choose the most concise revision: “The report makes a recommendation that the school should conduct a two-month trial.”

options.text: The report recommends a two-month trial.
The report makes a recommendation that the school should conduct a two-month trial.
options.whyWrong: 'Makes a recommendation that' can be replaced by the direct verb 'recommends'.

options.text: The report gives a recommendation in regard to the conducting of a two-month trial.
options.whyWrong: This turns a direct action into several abstract noun phrases.

options.text: A recommendation is made by the report for the purpose of a two-month trial.
options.whyWrong: The passive wording is longer and less direct.

explanation.whyCorrect: The direct verb 'recommends' preserves the meaning in far fewer words.
explanation.quickTip: Prefer strong direct verbs over noun-heavy phrases when no nuance is lost.

questions.prompt: The class observed lights left on; {{blank}}, the billing records cannot show how much those lights alone cost.

options.text: therefore
options.whyWrong: The limitation is not a result proving a cost figure.

options.text: for example
options.whyWrong: The billing limitation is not an example of observing lights left on.

options.text: however
similarly
options.whyWrong: The two statements have different roles; the second limits the first.

explanation.whyCorrect: 'However' introduces the important limitation on what the observation can establish.
explanation.quickTip: Use contrast transitions to signal a limit, exception, or difference.

options.text: Several factors can affect: the bill, weather, events, and equipment changes.
options.whyWrong: The colon incorrectly interrupts the verb and its object.

options.text: Several factors can affect the bill; weather, events, and equipment changes.
options.whyWrong: A semicolon does not introduce a simple list fragment.

options.text: Several factors can affect the bill, weather, events, and equipment changes.
options.whyWrong: The comma does not clearly signal that the following items are examples of the factors.

options.text: Several factors can affect the bill: weather, events, and equipment changes.

explanation.whyCorrect: The complete clause introduces a list, so the colon is appropriate.
explanation.quickTip: Place a colon after a complete statement, not between a verb and its object.

curriculum.learningObjective: Edit grammar, punctuation, usage, and clarity in passage context.
